strengths: Simple, elegant, and well-motivated contribution: a Riemannian metric on the diffusion noise space built from the score Jacobian, requiring no additional training or architectural modification, directly building on recent theoretical findings (Stanczuk et al., 2024; Ventura et al., 2025).

The discrete energy objective (Eq. 11) is particularly clean: minimizing the change of the score function along the path is numerically stable and simple to implement, and admits a natural interpretation as a pullback metric of the score function.

Comprehensive empirical validation across three settings: synthetic 2D data (with an interpretable density-consistency metric), image interpolation on three benchmarks against five baselines (LERP, SLERP, NAO, NoiseDiff, GeoDiff), and video frame interpolation with ground-truth middle frames — the latter providing more direct quantitative evidence than typical perceptual-only evaluations.

The method consistently outperforms the strongest baseline (GeoDiff) on FID, PPL, and RE in image interpolation and on MSE/LPIPS in video interpolation, with ablation studies (prompt adjustment, varying tau) and spectral analysis of the Jacobian in the appendix that support the design choices.

Honest and useful discussion of limitations: degeneracy of the metric at t=0, the local-minimizer nature of geodesics, dependence on initialization, and the non-symmetry of the learned Jacobian are all acknowledged and analyzed (Appendix A, D.3).
Reproducibility is well supported: detailed experimental setup, code attached as supplementary material, and proper attribution of the prompt-adjustment protocol to Yu et al. (2025).
weaknesses: Novelty concern relative to closely related work: Azeglio & Di Bernardo (2025) already propose a score-based Riemannian metric for diffusion models, and the theoretical justification (Proposition 1) is largely a direct consequence of Stanczuk et al. (2024) and Ventura et al. (2025); the paper distinguishes itself primarily through the manifold-parallel (rather than density-seeking) motivation, but the differentiation in the related-work discussion is brief and should be sharpened.

The formal metric machinery is somewhat over-layered relative to what is actually used: the discrete optimization objective never explicitly uses G = J^T J, only first differences of the score, so the 'Riemannian metric' framing is interpretive rather than algorithmically essential; a reader may question what the metric formulation adds beyond 'minimize score change along the path'.

Sensitivity to hyperparameters: performance depends on the choice of noise-space timestep (t = 0.6T, with Appendix D.3 showing substantial quality variation across tau), the number of discretization points, initialization via SLERP, and optimizer settings; the method may be fragile in practice and the paper does not quantify this sensitivity beyond qualitative visualizations.

Geodesics are only local minimizers and paths are initialized with SLERP, raising the possibility that some gains reflect optimization-dependent behavior rather than intrinsic geodesic structure; no analysis of path-length consistency across random restarts is provided.
Image-interpolation benchmarks use small curated sets (50 pairs per dataset) with subjective perceptual claims; statistical significance or variance across curated pairs is not reported.
Computational cost is higher than closed-form interpolants (LERP/SLERP); although comparable to GeoDiff, runtime/iteration-cost comparisons are not provided.

The theory contribution is modest: Proposition 1 and its Appendix A.2 derivation (idealized symmetric Hessian case) are elementary and largely derivative of prior results, with the practical non-symmetric case only argued informally.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, technically sound idea: a pullback-style Riemannian metric on the diffusion noise space built from the score Jacobian (G = J^T J), grounded in recent theoretical findings (Stanczuk et al. 2024; Ventura et al. 2025) about the spectral gap of the score Hessian encoding the data manifold's tangent/normal decomposition. This is a natural and elegant bridge between manifold-analysis theory and a practical task.
The method requires no retraining or architectural modification of the diffusion model, which makes it broadly applicable to pre-trained models.

Experimental coverage is reasonably thorough for the interpolation application: synthetic 2D illustration, image interpolation on three benchmarks (MorphBench-animation, Animal Faces-HQ, CelebA-HQ), and video frame interpolation with ground-truth middle frames on DAVIS/Human/RE10K, with the proposed method consistently ranking best or second-best across FID, PPL, PDV, RE, MSE, and LPIPS.

The paper includes useful analyses: an ablation on prompt adjustment (Table 4), sensitivity of the interpolation quality and the Jacobian spectrum to the choice of timestep τ (Figs. 7-8), and honest discussion of limitations (degenerate metric at t=0, local-minimizer issues, approximate validity of Proposition 1 when the score is learned rather than exact).

The manuscript is clearly written, with a well-organized related-work section that carefully distinguishes the approach from density-based (conformal-metric) interpolators like GeodesicDiffusion, and supplementary details plus code for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate rather than high. The construction is essentially the pullback of the Euclidean metric through the score function, which is very close to concurrent/prior work the paper itself cites (Azeglio & Bernardo 2025, 'A Score-Based Riemannian Metric to Explore the Data Manifold'; Lobashev et al. 2025 on Hessian geometry; Park et al. 2023a on Riemannian geometry of diffusion latents). The manuscript does not clearly articulate what is technically different from Azeglio & Bernardo beyond the manifold-alignment motivation, which weakens the novelty claim.

The theoretical content is thin. Proposition 1 is a near-trivial consequence of the assumed eigenspace decomposition, and its main assumption (symmetric, exact score/Hessian with clean tangent/normal split) does not hold for learned noise predictors; the paper acknowledges this and retreats to an 'approximately holds' argument without quantifying the gap. The synthetic 2D experiment partly compensates, but a more careful empirical validation of the tangent-alignment claim at intermediate t would strengthen the work.

The evaluation has notable weaknesses relative to the claims: (a) the video benchmarks are very small (21, 56, and 26 clips), so the quantitative gains may not be statistically robust (no error bars or significance tests anywhere); (b) only one backbone (Stable Diffusion v2.1-base) is tested; (c) perceptual superiority is largely asserted through proxy metrics (FID, PPL, PDV) that are imperfectly correlated with human perception — no human study is provided despite the paper's central claim being 'perceptually more natural transitions.'

Several important hyperparameters appear hand-tuned with limited justification: the interpolation timestep t = 0.6T, the number of discretization points N = 10, the Adam settings, and the specific negative prompt. The τ ∈ [0.4T, 0.6T] sweet spot is justified only empirically and qualitatively; a sensitivity or automatic-selection procedure would be more convincing.

Computational cost is under-analyzed. Computing the score Jacobian-vector products and optimizing 500 Adam iterations per interpolation path is substantially more expensive than LERP/SLERP; the paper notes cost qualitatively but gives no timing comparison against baselines, which matters for practical adoption.

The scope of the empirical validation is narrower than the framing: the metric is positioned as a general geometric characterization of the learned data manifold, but the only demonstrated application is interpolation (clustering and other metric-related tasks are deferred to future work). As an Algorithms/General contribution, the impact rests largely on one task family.

The method also relies on the prompt-adjustment trick borrowed from Yu et al. (2025) (500-1000 iterations of embedding optimization), which slightly undercuts the 'no further training' claim and makes the comparison setup somewhat entangled with the baseline's machinery.

strengths: The paper presents a clean, well-motivated idea: a Riemannian metric on the diffusion noise space defined as the pullback of the Euclidean metric through the score function (G = J^T J), connected to recent theoretical findings that the score Jacobian's spectral structure reveals the data manifold (Stanczuk et al., Ventura et al.). This is a conceptually natural way to bring pullback-metric geometry from VAEs/GANs to diffusion models without retraining.

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough for this line of work: synthetic 2D validation, image interpolation on three benchmarks against five relevant baselines (including the strongest competitor GeodesicDiffusion), and video frame interpolation with ground-truth middle frames, which provides a more objective evaluation than image interpolation alone. The proposed method consistently achieves the best or near-best results (Table 2, Table 3).

The paper is honest about its assumptions and limitations: degeneracy of the metric at t=0, the need for a good initialization, the approximate nature of Proposition 1 when the score is not an exact gradient, and the sensitivity to the interpolation timestep. The ablation on prompt adjustment (Table 4), the visualization of singular value spectra across timesteps (Fig. 8), and the analysis of varying τ (Appendix D.3) strengthen the empirical case.

Geodesic computation via the discrete energy (Eq. 11) is simple, numerically stable, and avoids solving the second-order geodesic ODE; the reduction to minimizing score changes along the path is elegant and easy to implement.
Reproducibility is addressed well: detailed experimental setup in appendices, source code attached as supplementary material.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate and the conceptual core is close to existing work. The metric is a straightforward pullback through the score function, and the manifold interpretation is imported from Stanczuk et al. (2024) and Ventura et al. (2025). Most importantly, Azeglio & Di Bernardo (2025) propose a 'Score-Based Riemannian Metric to Explore the Data Manifold', which appears very similar in spirit; the manuscript cites this work only in the context of density-prioritizing metrics and does not clearly differentiate its contribution from it. A sharper comparison or discussion is needed to establish what is genuinely new.

Proposition 1 is mathematically elementary (minimizing ||Jv|| under fixed norm favors the small-singular-value subspace), and the claimed behavior that 'geodesics stay within or run parallel to the data manifold' is a heuristic interpretation rather than a proven property. No theory connects the discrete objective (Eq. 11) to actual geodesics of the claimed manifold structure beyond local intuition.

Evaluation scale is small: 50 curated image pairs per dataset (LPIPS < 0.6 filtering), yielding roughly 500 interpolated images for FID computation. FID on such tiny sets is statistically fragile, and the headline claim of 'perceptually more natural and faithful transitions' is supported only by automatic metrics and a handful of qualitative figures, with no human evaluation or user study.

The method requires tuning the interpolation timestep τ (empirically 0.4T–0.6T), and this selection appears to be based on visual quality on datasets (e.g., CelebA-HQ in Fig. 7) that overlap with the evaluation sets, raising a mild risk of test-set tuning. Computational cost of the path optimization (500 Adam iterations on ~16k-dimensional intermediate points per pair) is acknowledged qualitatively but no wall-clock comparison to baselines is reported.

The quantitative margins over the strongest baseline (GeodesicDiffusion) on image interpolation are modest (e.g., FID 27.44 vs 28.70 on MB(A); PPL 0.380 vs 0.402), and without variance estimates or significance testing it is hard to judge whether the differences are meaningful. The video interpolation gains are larger and more convincing.

strengths: The core idea is original and well-motivated: instead of building diffusion geodesics on density (which is known to produce over-smoothed results), the paper uses the spectral structure of the score Jacobian (Stanczuk et al., 2024; Ventura et al., 2025) to define a pullback metric that separates tangent from normal directions. This is a principled and conceptually satisfying answer to the question posed in the introduction.

The derivation is clean: the energy functional admits an elegant equivalent reading (minimizing squared score variation along the path), and the contrast with the rank-1 FIM-based metric of Azeglio & Bernardo (2025) is well argued — the distinction matters because real-world manifolds have codimension greater than one.

Validation is unusually thorough and complementary: (i) a synthetic 2D experiment with a quantifiable manifold-consistency measure; (ii) image interpolation on four benchmarks against six baselines including the two most relevant prior metrics; (iii) video frame interpolation against ground-truth middle frames, which provides an objective (not merely perceptual) proxy that prior interpolation papers lack; (iv) guidance correction evaluated with FID/CLIP over 30k images; (v) transfer to distilled models at no student-side cost.

Statistical rigor is above average: one-sided exact binomial tests for improvements over the second-best method, seed-matched distillation runs across five trials, and extensive ablations (noise level τ with singular-value visualizations, CG weight λ robustness, CG iteration count, prompt adjustment) plus a second backbone (SD v2.0-base) confirming generality.

The guidance-correction application is practical and cleverly designed: it modifies only the guidance term, requires four extra score evaluations via Jacobian-vector products approximated by finite differences, and is inheritable by the student in distillation. The spectral-gap analysis explaining robustness to λ is a nice touch.

The paper is honest about limitations and open questions (approximate symmetry of the Jacobian, degeneracy at t=0, need for validation on newer architectures), and reproducibility appears good given detailed hyperparameters, prompts, and cost analysis (Table 6).
weaknesses: The theoretical claims rest on approximations that are acknowledged but not fully controlled: the score Jacobian is not symmetric in practice (the tangent/normal decomposition and Proposition 1 hold only 'approximately'), and positive definiteness of G is argued empirically rather than guaranteed. The spectral-gap evidence (Fig. 11) is shown only for CelebA-HQ on one backbone; a systematic characterization across datasets would strengthen the geometric claim.

Computational cost is a real limitation: geodesic computation needs 500 Adam iterations per path, and guidance correction roughly triples per-step cost (Table 13 shows 2→6 NFE). The paper describes this transparently and it is comparable to prior metric-based methods, but it limits practicality relative to closed-form baselines.

The practical gains of guidance correction over CFG are modest in absolute terms (FID 14.29→13.81 at w=7.5; 17.28→16.04 at w=12.5), and the method does not consistently beat CFG++ at all scales. The evidence of improvement is consistency and significance rather than magnitude, which slightly weakens the impact claim of this application.

On PDV, the proposed method is second-best (losing to SLERP) on three of four datasets in both Table 2 and the v2.0 results; the claim of uniformly capturing geometry would be cleaner if this were explained.

Evaluation metrics for interpolation (PPL, PDV, FID, RE) are, as the authors themselves concede, indirect proxies for manifold faithfulness; the paper mitigates this well with the video ground-truth experiment, but a direct probe of the tangent–normal decomposition accuracy (e.g., comparing estimated tangent spaces against controlled synthetic manifolds of known dimension beyond 2D) is missing.

Experiments are limited to Stable Diffusion v2.x backbones and DDPM/DDIM-family models; the authors correctly note that validation on more recent architectures (SDXL, flow-matching models) is future work, but for a paper whose central claim is a general geometric tool, this narrows the demonstrated scope.

strengths: The core idea is clear and well-motivated: while prior diffusion-geodesic methods (density-based, FIM-based) guide paths toward high-density regions, the proposed metric G = J^T J built from the score Jacobian exploits the tangent/normal spectral gap (Stanczuk et al., 2024; Ventura et al., 2025), yielding a geometrically principled alternative that is training-free and architecture-agnostic.

The paper is honest about the limits of its evidence: it explicitly acknowledges that PPL/PDV/FID/RE are indirect proxies for manifold faithfulness and therefore complements image interpolation with a ground-truth video frame interpolation evaluation (Table 3), which strengthens the validation considerably.

Experimental coverage is broad and thorough: synthetic 2D, image interpolation on four benchmarks, video frame interpolation on three benchmarks, CFG correction at multiple guidance scales, distillation transfer to LCM, a second backbone (SD v2.0-base), and ablations on τ, λ, CG iterations, and prompt adjustment, with one-sided exact binomial significance tests reported.

The method-to-algorithm bridge is well worked out: the discrete energy (eq. 3), the CG-based guidance correction with Jacobian-vector-product approximations (eq. 5), and computational cost analysis (Table 6) make the approach reproducible and practically grounded.

The theoretical remarks are appropriately cautious: the authors correctly note that the learned score Jacobian is not exactly symmetric, that the tangent/normal decomposition holds only approximately, and they connect the FIM-based metric's rank-1 limitation to the codimension of real data manifolds.

Interpolation results are consistent: the method achieves the best PPL, FID, and RE across all datasets (Tables 2 and 9) and the best MSE/LPIPS on all video benchmarks, with a plausible qualitative explanation for baseline failures (density-based geodesics over-smooth; FIM-based metric is nearly singular).
weaknesses: The novelty is largely in the combination and application: the key spectral-gap insight is taken directly from Stanczuk et al. (2024) and Ventura et al. (2025), and the construction G = J^T J is a standard pullback metric. Proposition 1 and the derivation in B.1 are straightforward given that prior work; the theoretical contribution is modest.

The computational cost is significant and not fully confronted in the main narrative: interpolation requires ~500 optimization iterations plus DDIM inversion and full denoising per path, and the guidance correction triples NFE per denoising step (Table 13: NFE 2 → 6). This limits practical appeal relative to closed-form baselines like SLERP, and head-to-head comparisons do not control for this compute disparity.

Evaluation metrics remain imperfect for the central claim of 'manifold faithfulness.' The paper admits none of PPL/PDV/FID/RE directly measures geometry; the video frame interpolation task is a reasonable but imperfect proxy (frame-2 prediction conflates manifold adherence with simple motion smoothness), and the acknowledged mismatch between quantitative scores and visual quality for small τ (E.3) suggests the metrics may reward blending artifacts.

The quantitative gains over the strongest baseline (GeoDiff) are consistent but modest in absolute terms (e.g., FID 27.44 vs 28.70 on MB(A); MSE improvements on small clip counts of 21/56/26 videos), and the guidance-correction FID improvements (e.g., 14.29 → 13.81 at w=7.5) are small relative to the 3x inference cost.

The empirical assumption that the score Jacobian is approximately symmetric (used for vector-Jacobian products via finite differences) is asserted as 'empirically supported' but is never directly quantified; error accumulation in CG iterations (performance degrades at 3 iterations) suggests this approximation is a real fragility.

Validation is confined to one model family (SD v2.0/v2.1) and image latent spaces; the authors themselves note that validating on more recent architectures (e.g., DiT/flow-matching models) remains future work, which constrains demonstrated generality.

Some experimental choices merit more justification: operation at τ = 0.6T is chosen partly because MSE/LPIPS 'do not align' with visual quality at smaller τ, introducing a subjective element into hyperparameter selection; the curated 50-pair subsets with LPIPS < 0.6 filtering are small and selection criteria could bias toward easy cases.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and principled: rather than defining a diffusion-model metric from density (which conflates manifold location with orientation, as the paper convincingly argues), the authors build a pullback metric J^T J from the score Jacobian, directly leveraging the recently established spectral characterization of tangent/normal directions (Stanczuk et al., Ventura et al.). This is a natural but non-obvious extension of latent pullback metrics (VAEs/GANs) to the over-complete noise space of diffusion models.

The work demonstrates the metric from two complementary angles — global geometry (geodesic interpolation) and local geometry (tangent–normal projection for CFG correction) — which strengthens the validation that the metric reflects actual manifold geometry rather than merely optimizing an interpolation heuristic.

Experiments are broad and reasonably rigorous: synthetic 2D data with a density-variation metric, image interpolation on four benchmarks against six baselines, video frame interpolation against ground-truth middle frames (a genuinely objective proxy that most interpolation papers lack), generation with CFG correction, and distillation transfer. Statistical significance tests are reported, a second backbone (SD v2.0) is evaluated, and ablations cover prompt adjustment, noise level tau, CG weight, and CG iterations.
The method is training-free and requires no architectural modification; the guidance-correction variant also transfers to distilled models at no inference cost, which is practically meaningful.

The paper is clearly written, with honest discussion of approximations (non-symmetric Jacobian, finite-difference JVPs, single CG step), and the theoretical remarks distinguishing the full-spectrum metric from rank-1 FIM metrics are well argued.
weaknesses: The core construction is mathematically simple — a pullback of the Euclidean metric through the score map — and its validity rests almost entirely on prior spectral-gap results rather than new theory. Proposition 1 and its derivation (Sec. B.1) are essentially direct consequences of the cited spectral decomposition; the 'theoretical contribution' framing should be tempered accordingly.

The guidance-correction gains, while consistent, are modest (e.g., FID 13.81 vs 14.29 for CFG at w=7.5, and the CFG++ baseline is within noise), and the method costs roughly 3x the NFE per denoising step. A stronger or at least newer guidance baseline (e.g., TCFG, which is discussed in related work but not compared) would better support the practical significance claim.

Interpolation evaluation metrics (PPL, PDV, FID on ~900 images) are indirect proxies for manifold faithfulness, which the authors acknowledge; the strongest evidence comes from the video ground-truth experiments, but these are limited to three-frame clips at 512x512 and are not a fair comparison to dedicated video interpolation methods.

The iterative geodesic optimization (500 Adam iterations with Jacobian-vector products per step) makes the method noticeably more expensive than closed-form baselines; a runtime/quality trade-off table in the main text would help readers assess practicality.

Some claims are under-supported: 'positive definite in practice' is asserted rather than empirically verified across datasets/timesteps; the approximate symmetry of the Jacobian ('empirically supported') is not quantified; and the assumption that the JVP via finite differences plus a transposed version approximates the vector-Jacobian product deserves error analysis, especially since CG degradation at 3 iterations is attributed to this approximation.

No code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned in the manuscript, which is a concern given the many implementation details (prompt adjustment, hyperparameters, curated image pairs) that affect results.
No societal-impact discussion, though the method itself poses limited direct risk given it operates on pre-trained generative models.
